j.learned_fact: Rabbit teeth grow continuously and are worn down by chewing grass and plants — true.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (chewing wears teeth down)
j.notes: Two lessons (print conventions + rabbit teeth) compete, and the mother's "books start at the front" line is bolted on; the story-within-a-story frame is abstract for a 4-year-old, and Amelia's explicit conclusion sounds adult.

j.learned_fact: An empty tummy growls when you are hungry, and hot soup must be cooled/blown on; stoves are hot and not to be touched. All accurate.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (empty tummy → growling; blowing → cooler food)
j.notes: Very slight plot — waiting for dinner — with the safety lesson ("She did not touch the hot stove") slightly bolted on. Pleasant and age-appropriate but low stakes and minimal new learning.

j.learned_fact: Five senses matched to body parts (eyes see, nose smells, ears hear, tongue tastes); the claim that vibrations travel to the eardrum and make it shake is true but the phrase "the table is wiggling air" and a 3-year-old explaining eardrums is not age-appropriate.
j.thinking_skill: links a felt vibration to a heard sound
j.notes: Reads like a senses checklist with a bolted-on eardrum lecture spoken implausibly by a toddler; "Her problem was solved" refers to a problem that was never posed, and "lucky to have such a good dinner" is a stray moral.

j.learned_fact: Red and blue mixed together make purple; bread dough rises because tiny living things (yeast) eat sugar and make bubbles.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (mixing two colours makes a third)
j.notes: Two separate lessons are packed into a short piece, and the baker's yeast explanation ("tiny living things eating the sugar and making bubbles", plus the confusing squishing aside) is delivered as adult exposition well above a 3-year-old's grasp. The colour-mixing half fits the age nicely; the bakery half does not.

j.learned_fact: Sweat comes out of the skin and cools you as it dries (evaporative cooling) — accurate, though simplified.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (drop dries, face feels cooler)
j.notes: Charming voice ("My face is leaking!"), but the evaporation explanation and the hot-water safety aside are abstract for a 3-year-old; two lessons crowd a very short piece, and there is no repetition or rhythm to support pre-readers.

j.learned_fact: When you push the toilet handle, water rushes from the tank into the bowl and down the pipe — accurate, though barely explained.
j.thinking_skill: notices a simple cause and effect (push handle → water goes down)
j.notes: Two unrelated mini-episodes (zipping a coat, flushing a toilet) are stitched together by an arbitrary summary line that implies a connection that doesn't exist; the toy sheep serves no purpose. Language and repetition ("up, up, up", "whoosh") suit a three-year-old well.

j.learned_fact: A fridge cools its inside by moving heat out to the back, which is why the back feels warm — accurate, but delivered as an adult explanation.
j.thinking_skill: notices a surprising observation and accepts an explanation for it
j.notes: Two unrelated episodes (fridge heat, tablet drawing) stitched together with an irrelevant bus picture; the science is a librarian's mini-lecture rather than something Miles figures out, and heat transfer is beyond a four-year-old.

j.learned_fact: A letter needs an address so the mail carrier can deliver it; mail goes to a sorting building before reaching the recipient.
j.thinking_skill: notices a missing step and fixes it (letter needs an address)
j.notes: Clear and warm, but vocabulary ("address", "mail carrier", "envelope", "seal") and the several-step postal sequence sit above a 3-year-old; no repetition or sound play to anchor a JK listener.

j.learned_fact: A scab is like a lid that protects the knee while new skin grows underneath, so you shouldn't pick it.
j.thinking_skill: applies a simple rule (don't pick, skin heals underneath)
j.notes: Sara delivers the scab explanation as a mini-lecture, and a 3-year-old peer explaining skin biology is unconvincing; the bear-story and bandage-shop bits are filler that break focus. Vocabulary is mostly fine for age 3 but "librarian," "excited," "bandages" and the metaphor of a "lid" stretch it.

j.learned_fact: Fog is a cloud that sits on the ground, made of tiny water drops — accurate.
j.thinking_skill: recognizes that two things (fog and cloud) are the same kind of thing
j.notes: The time structure (yesterday/today/later) and the abstract insight are beyond a 3-year-old; "The problem was solved" is a flat narrator-ish line that breaks the child's voice.

j.learned_fact: Six cookies shared one-by-one between two people gives three each (fair sharing by dealing out); pressing too hard tears toast.
j.thinking_skill: notices cause and effect, then adjusts; shares by one-to-one dealing
j.notes: Charlie's dialogue ("It tore because I pushed too hard", "How can we fix it?") is a bit too tidily explanatory for a four-year-old; the three episodes feel like a skills checklist strung together rather than one story.

j.learned_fact: You pay money for things in a store, and the store uses that money to buy more goods and pay workers.
j.thinking_skill: restates a simple cause and effect (money buys goods, store restocks)
j.notes: Grandpa's explanation about paying workers and restocking is an adult-voiced mini-lecture, and Madeline's neat summary line is beyond a three-year-old's speech; otherwise sentences are short and age-appropriate.

j.learned_fact: Sweat on the skin dries and that drying makes you feel cooler; hats and shade help keep you cool.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (sitting in shade → water dries → feels cool)
j.notes: The word "sweat" is never used, so the key concept stays vague, and a three-year-old declaring "My skin lets the water out" is an adult explanation in a child's mouth. The hat/"stay close to me" ending is tacked on and doesn't follow from the sweat discovery.

j.learned_fact: Sharing by dealing out one item at a time makes equal groups — but the arithmetic is wrong: six cookies cannot give Ben three, Sam three, and Alice three (that needs nine).
j.thinking_skill: deals out items one-by-one to make equal shares
j.notes: The core math fails: six cookies are distributed but three children end up with three each, and the counting line "two, three, four" doesn't track the giving. For a counting story, that error is fatal.

j.learned_fact: A scab is like a lid that protects while new skin grows underneath — accurate.
j.thinking_skill: delays gratification and connects waiting to a later result
j.notes: The stadium setting is filler unconnected to the scab thread, and phrases like "At the last minute of the game" and "tummy felt jumpy and excited" are above a 3-year-old's grasp; counting line feels bolted on.

j.learned_fact: A letter needs an address so the mail carrier knows where to deliver it; mail goes to a sorting building before reaching the house.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (no address = can't deliver)
j.notes: The ending drifts (apples, bread, "took turns buying") and Emilia's line "Because the address tells where" is stilted, adult-sounding reasoning rather than a 3-year-old's voice; "present picture" is odd phrasing.

j.learned_fact: Rabbits' front teeth never stop growing, so they chew tough plants to wear them down — accurate.
j.thinking_skill: matches body parts to their senses; links long teeth to a need for chewing
j.notes: Two lessons bolted together (senses drill, then a Mom-delivered fact paragraph); "Her back leaned on the chair" is a stray, confusing line, and Mom's explanation is too dense for age 4.

j.learned_fact: Sound travels as vibrations that make the eardrum shake — accurate, though "sound is air wiggling" is incomplete since here it travels through water.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (wiggles in water → hearing)
j.notes: Two unrelated threads (the shy boy plot is dropped after one line; then a science lesson) with no real story arc; Daddy's eardrum explanation is a bolted-on definition too abstract for a three-year-old, though the repeated "kick, kick, splash" fits.

j.learned_fact: Squares have four sides; triangles have three — accurate.
j.thinking_skill: counts and sorts shapes by number of sides; adjusts action after a slip
j.notes: Pleasant and age-appropriate, but the plot is just a snack routine with no real problem; the "crackers standing like walls" detail goes nowhere and the ending is flat.

j.learned_fact: Cutting an onion releases a gas that makes eyes sting and water — this is true, though the story calls it only "gas" without naming it.
j.thinking_skill: weighs two explanations for Dad's tears (sadness vs. onion)
j.notes: Pronoun slip ("Her tears came because of the gas") muddles whose eyes water, and a nurse chopping onions at a clinic table is implausible; words like "clinic," "gas," "stinging" and the shot-anxiety theme sit above a 4-year-old's comfort, though the counting and sticker ending fit.
